Interpreting impacts

Source: vignettes/impacts.Rmd
impacts.Rmd

The coefficients of a spatial probit model are not marginal effects. Three things stand between a coefficient and the change in a probability:

  1. the spatial multiplier: a change in unit jj’s regressor moves jj’s latent outcome, which moves its neighbours’ through ρW\rho W, which moves their neighbours’, and so on;
  2. the probit link: a change in the latent outcome moves the probability by an amount that depends on where the unit sits on the normal curve;
  3. the scale of the latent outcome: the spatial process and the random effects add variance to the latent outcome, so a unit change in it moves the probability less than in a plain probit.

This vignette explains what psp_impacts() computes, how the answer depends on the model, and how to work with the draws. vignette("getting-started") has the short version.

library(panelspatialprobit)
W <- psp_weights(rook_weights(7, 7), style = "W")
ctrl <- psp_control(iter = 3000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2, seed = 1, progress = FALSE)

What is computed

Write S=I−ρWS = I - \rho W. Integrating out the random effects, the latent outcome of period tt has mean mt=S−1(Xtβ+WXtθ)m_t = S^{-1}(X_t\beta + WX_t\theta) and the standard deviation of unit ii’s latent outcome is si=(1+σα2)[S−1S−⊤]iis_i = \sqrt{(1 + \sigma_\alpha^2)\,[S^{-1}S^{-\top}]_{ii}} (with spatial errors, S−1R−1S^{-1}R^{-1} takes the place of S−1S^{-1} in the error part). So P(yit=1)=Φ(mit/si)P(y_{it} = 1) = \Phi(m_{it}/s_i) and

∂P(yit=1)∂xjt,r=ϕ(mit/si)si[S−1(βrI+θrW)]ij.\frac{\partial P(y_{it} = 1)}{\partial x_{jt,r}} = \frac{\phi(m_{it}/s_i)}{s_i}\,\big[S^{-1}(\beta_r I + \theta_r W)\big]_{ij}.

This is an N×NN \times N matrix of effects for every regressor, period and posterior draw. Following LeSage and Pace (2009), it is summarised by three averages:

  • direct: the average diagonal element, the effect of a unit’s own regressor on its own probability (including the feedback that returns to it through its neighbours);
  • total: the average row sum, the effect on a unit’s probability of the same change in the regressor of every unit;
  • indirect: total minus direct, the spillover.

The averages run over units and periods; by_period = TRUE also reports them period by period. Every quantity is computed for each posterior draw, so the impacts come with posterior intervals.

A spatial Durbin example

We simulate data in which x1x_1 also acts through the neighbours’ values (θ1=0.5\theta_1 = 0.5) and x2x_2 does not (θ2=0\theta_2 = 0), and fit a spatial Durbin model:

d <- sim_psprobit(W, T = 5, beta = c(-0.2, 1, -0.8), theta = c(0.5, 0), rho = 0.4,
                  sigma_alpha = 0.7, seed = 1)
fit <- psprobit(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d, index = c("id", "time"), W = W,
                model = "sdm", control = ctrl)
fit$impacts
#> Impacts on P(y = 1) (posterior mean, sd, 95% interval; 500 draws)
#> 
#> direct:
#>       mean     sd    q2.5   q97.5
#> x1  0.1876 0.0201  0.1470  0.2238
#> x2 -0.1407 0.0200 -0.1766 -0.1032
#> 
#> indirect:
#>       mean     sd    q2.5  q97.5
#> x1  0.2918 0.0574  0.1731 0.4065
#> x2 -0.0707 0.0532 -0.1692 0.0367
#> 
#> total:
#>       mean     sd    q2.5   q97.5
#> x1  0.4794 0.0577  0.3688  0.5914
#> x2 -0.2114 0.0596 -0.3306 -0.1002

The spillover of x1x_1 is larger than its direct effect: its own Durbin term adds to the multiplier. In a SAR model (no θ\theta) the matrix in brackets is βrS−1\beta_r S^{-1} for every regressor, so the ratio of indirect to direct impacts is the same for all regressors. That is a strong restriction; the Durbin terms relax it.

Which models have spillovers

The model fixes which channels exist:

model spillovers through indirect impacts
"sar" ρ\rho: global (all units, decaying with distance) yes, same ratio for all regressors
"sdm" ρ\rho and θ\theta yes, free ratio
"slx" θ\theta only: neighbours of the changed unit local only
"sdem" θ\theta only; λ\lambda is in the errors local only
"sem" none; λ\lambda is in the errors zero
"sarar" ρ\rho as "sar"

A spatial error term (λ\lambda) does not carry a change in a regressor from one unit to another; it only changes sis_i. The SEM’s indirect impacts are therefore exactly zero:

fit_sem <- psprobit(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d, index = c("id", "time"), W = W,
                    model = "sem", control = ctrl)
fit_sem$impacts
#> Impacts on P(y = 1) (posterior mean, sd, 95% interval; 500 draws)
#> 
#> direct:
#>       mean     sd    q2.5   q97.5
#> x1  0.1880 0.0267  0.1373  0.2378
#> x2 -0.1492 0.0219 -0.1910 -0.1038
#> 
#> indirect:
#>    mean sd q2.5 q97.5
#> x1    0  0    0     0
#> x2    0  0    0     0
#> 
#> total:
#>       mean     sd    q2.5   q97.5
#> x1  0.1880 0.0267  0.1373  0.2378
#> x2 -0.1492 0.0219 -0.1910 -0.1038

Here the SEM is the wrong model: it attributes the spillover of x1x_1 to nothing, and its direct impacts are close to the SDM’s. With real data, compare the specifications with psp_ppc() and psp_dic() (see vignette("getting-started")) rather than choosing by the size of the impacts.

The scale

The division by sis_i matters. In a plain probit the latent error has variance one, so β\beta is measured in standard deviations of the latent outcome. Here the variance of the latent outcome is larger, by the factor (1+σα2)[S−1S−⊤]ii(1 + \sigma_\alpha^2)[S^{-1}S^{-\top}]_{ii}, and a probability changes less for the same latent change. The spatialprobit package (Wilhelm and de Matos 2013) leaves this factor out (P=Φ(mit)P = \Phi(m_{it})). scale = "lesage_pace" reproduces its convention, for comparison with published results:

psp_impacts(fit, scale = "lesage_pace")
#> Impacts on P(y = 1) (posterior mean, sd, 95% interval; 500 draws)
#> Scale: LeSage-Pace (no reduced-form sd)
#> 
#> direct:
#>       mean     sd    q2.5   q97.5
#> x1  0.2151 0.0222  0.1701  0.2532
#> x2 -0.1613 0.0221 -0.2040 -0.1182
#> 
#> indirect:
#>       mean     sd    q2.5  q97.5
#> x1  0.3352 0.0684  0.1989 0.4751
#> x2 -0.0809 0.0611 -0.1898 0.0440
#> 
#> total:
#>       mean     sd    q2.5   q97.5
#> x1  0.5503 0.0694  0.4245  0.6896
#> x2 -0.2422 0.0677 -0.3815 -0.1130

The impacts are larger, because they ignore the extra variance. The default ("reduced_form") gives the derivatives of the probabilities the model actually implies; we recommend it for interpretation.

Population and unit impacts

The population impacts integrate the random effects out: they describe a population of units like those in the sample. type = "unit" instead conditions on the posterior draws of the random effects, so that mt=S−1(Xtβ+WXtθ+α)m_t = S^{-1}(X_t\beta + WX_t\theta + \alpha) and si2=[S−1S−⊤]iis_i^2 = [S^{-1}S^{-\top}]_{ii}. These are the impacts for the units in the sample:

psp_impacts(fit, type = "unit", draws = 300)
#> Impacts on P(y = 1) (posterior mean, sd, 95% interval; 300 draws)
#> Unit-specific (conditional on the random effects)
#> 
#> direct:
#>       mean     sd   q2.5   q97.5
#> x1  0.1983 0.0211  0.155  0.2384
#> x2 -0.1509 0.0226 -0.191 -0.1004
#> 
#> indirect:
#>       mean     sd    q2.5  q97.5
#> x1  0.3014 0.0643  0.1748 0.4324
#> x2 -0.0736 0.0564 -0.1849 0.0339
#> 
#> total:
#>       mean     sd    q2.5   q97.5
#> x1  0.4996 0.0641  0.3732  0.6347
#> x2 -0.2245 0.0642 -0.3421 -0.1015

Unit impacts are larger than population impacts. A unit with a known random effect has less latent uncertainty left, so its probability responds more sharply. Averaging over the random effects flattens the response. Both are correct answers to different questions.

Working with the draws

imp$draws is an array with dimensions draw × variable × category × effect, so any derived quantity gets a posterior distribution. For example, the share of the total effect of x1x_1 that is spillover:

dr <- fit$impacts$draws
share <- dr[, "x1", 1, "indirect"] / dr[, "x1", 1, "total"]
quantile(share, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
#>        5%       50%       95% 
#> 0.5081829 0.6107099 0.6926877

summary(imp) returns the table as a data frame, one row per variable, category and effect (and period with by_period = TRUE).

Ordered outcomes

For an ordered model the impacts are computed for every category: ∂P(yit=k)/∂xjt,r\partial P(y_{it} = k)/\partial x_{jt,r}. Raising a regressor with a positive coefficient lowers the probabilities of the low categories and raises those of the high ones, and the impacts sum to zero over categories. See vignette("ordered-outcomes").

Derivatives and discrete changes

Impacts are derivatives: they describe small changes. For a discrete change, such as a policy that raises x1x_1 by one unit everywhere, compare predictions directly. predict(newdata = ) takes the same units and periods with new regressor values:

d_up <- d
d_up$x1 <- d_up$x1 + 1
mean(predict(fit, newdata = d_up) - predict(fit))
#> [1] 0.4275649

The average change in probability is close to the total impact of x1x_1 above, but smaller: probabilities are bounded, and the normal curve flattens as units move into the tails. For changes of more than a fraction of a standard deviation of the regressor, prefer the discrete comparison.

Changing the regressor for some units only works the same way: the predicted change for the other units is then their spillover.

Dynamic models

With a lagged outcome, the impacts above are short-run: they describe the period in which the regressor changes. The change also works through later periods via the outcome history. psp_response_path() traces that; see vignette("dynamics").

References

LeSage, J. P. and Pace, R. K. (2009). Introduction to Spatial Econometrics. CRC Press.

Wilhelm, S. and de Matos, M. G. (2013). Estimating spatial probit models in R. The R Journal 5(1), 130–143.
